c.tagline: Haiti's colonial second city, gateway to the mountaintop Citadelle and Sans-Souci Palace.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps; getting around means shared tap-taps (converted pickups on fixed routes) and moto-taxis, or a private car hired through your hotel. Fares are unmetered and negotiated first — US dollars are accepted almost everywhere alongside the gourde.

emergency.note: Formal emergency services are limited and many visitors rely on their hotel or a private driver; check your government's current Haiti travel advisory before going.

avoid.reason: Avoid all road travel toward Port-au-Prince and isolated areas outside the city; while Cap-Haïtien is calmer than the capital, check current security conditions as gang activity fluctuates.
Petty theft occurs in the Marché de Fer market area and crowded streets — keep valuables out of sight and avoid walking after dark.

hood_desc: Cap-Haïtien's tightly gridded colonial core around the Place d'Armes and the twin-towered Notre-Dame Cathedral, full of gingerbread balconies, the Iron Market, and street life; the walkable base for most visitors.
The breezy seafront district along the Boulevard du Carénage, where locals stroll, eat, and watch the harbour; a lively, central place to stay near the water.
A sprawling, densely populated fishing and residential zone east of the centre across the bay; authentic and local, with few tourist services.
The city's southern gateway rising toward Fort Vertières, monument to the 1803 battle that sealed Haiti's independence; mostly residential and historically significant rather than touristy.
The resort-and-beach coast west of town toward Labadie, home to Cormier Plage and quiet cove hotels; a relaxed seaside base away from the city bustle.

water.note: Drink only bottled or treated water; cholera outbreaks have occurred.

transit.hours: Tap-taps and moto-taxis run through daylight and into the evening; service thins after dark.
transit.note: Cap-Haïtien has no formal bus or rail network. Shared tap-taps (brightly painted pickups on fixed routes) and moto-taxis are the everyday transport, alongside private hired cars.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash — gourdes or US dollars — as you get off a tap-tap (a few gourdes per hop); moto-taxi and private fares are negotiated first.

bus: Tap-tap shared taxis around the city
Long-distance buses and vans to Port-au-Prince via national highways
ferry: Occasional coastal boats to Labadie and nearby beaches

transit.m: Taxi or hotel shuttle to the city centre (10-15 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants where service isn't already added; small tips to guides and drivers are appreciated.

landmarks: Citadelle Laferrière
The Western Hemisphere's largest fortress crowns a 900-meter peak with 365 cannons, King Henri Christophe's UNESCO-listed monument to Haitian independence and defiance.
Sans-Souci Palace
The haunting ruins of Christophe's 'Versailles of the Caribbean' at Milot, a once-opulent royal palace shattered by the 1842 earthquake yet still magnificent.
Cathédrale Notre-Dame du Cap-Haïtien
A gleaming white domed cathedral on Place d'Armes, rebuilt in the 1940s, that has witnessed coronations, revolutions, and daily life since colonial Cap-Français.
Place d'Armes
The historic main square of old Cap-Français, where independence-era proclamations rang out, now framed by the cathedral, gingerbread balconies, and lively street vendors.
Historic Center Gingerbread Streets
Grid-planned colonial streets lined with wrought-iron balconies, arcades, and faded pastel townhouses recall the city's era as the 'Paris of the Antilles'.
Monument des Héros de Vertières
This stirring memorial marks the 1803 Battle of Vertières, where Dessalines' army defeated Napoleon's forces to seal the world's only successful slave revolution.
Labadee Peninsula
A jaw-dropping stretch of jungle-backed coves and coral waters just west of the city, famed for beaches like Paradise Cove and its private cruise resort.
Île-à-Rat (Amiga Island)
A tiny white-sand islet floating in translucent turquoise water offshore, reached by boat for snorkeling over coral gardens and grilled-lobster picnics.
Plage Cormier
A palm-fringed golden beach on the scenic coastal road to Labadee, home to a storied boutique resort and calm swimming waters.
Site des Ramiers
Four small forts on a plateau below the Citadelle, part of the UNESCO National History Park, offering hushed ruins and panoramic mountain views.

train.note: Haiti has no railway of any kind in operation. The sugar and plantation lines that ran between 1876 and 1991 have all closed and the track has largely been lifted, and there was never a cross-border rail connection to the Dominican Republic. All surface travel from Cap-Haïtien is by road or by boat.

intl.to: Dajabón (Dominican Republic) - cross on foot at the Ouanaminthe/Dajabón bridge, then Dominican coaches onward to Santiago and Santo Domingo

bus.note: The usual overland route out of Cap-Haïtien is a shared taxi or minibus east to Ouanaminthe (about 2 hours), walking across the Massacre River bridge into Dajabón, and picking up a Caribe Tours or Caribe Express coach onward to Santiago and Santo Domingo. Through international services have repeatedly been suspended since the Dominican Republic closed the border in late 2023, and the crossing itself has opened and shut at short notice, so check the current status before setting out. Domestically, tap-taps and minibuses use the informal stands around the Barrière Bouteille area rather than a formal terminal, and there is no online booking. The RN1 road south to Port-au-Prince (6-8 hours in good times) has been repeatedly cut by armed groups, so most travellers fly or avoid the route entirely; check your government's travel advice, as much of Haiti is under a do-not-travel warning.

intl.to: Port-au-Prince (Haiti) - coastal passenger boats from the Cap-Haïtien wharf, running irregularly and mainly when the RN1 road is blocked
intl.op: informal local boat operators — tickets bought at the wharf

ferry.note: Cap-Haïtien has a working port used mainly by cargo ships, and there is no scheduled international ferry to the Dominican Republic, Cuba, the Turks and Caicos or anywhere else. Coastal boats to Port-au-Prince and along the north coast are small, unscheduled and sold at the quayside; they appear and disappear according to demand and the state of the roads, and safety standards are poor. Royal Caribbean's private resort at Labadee, 10 km west, is served only by cruise ships and cannot be used for point-to-point travel. Small sailing boats also link the offshore islands, but nothing runs to a published timetable.

half.name: Fort Liberté
half.blurb: Coastal town on a lagoon with 18th-century French colonial fort ruins and a well-preserved historic center.

half.name: Limonade
half.blurb: Farming town surrounded by bitter-orange groves that supply zest for liqueurs like Grand Marnier and Cointreau.
